Chapter 5: Wrestling with Belonging and the Pull of Home.
There’s a quiet ache that settles in after years of living between two worlds. Maybe you know the feeling—the city that once seemed so strange now fits like a second skin. The streets, the little shops, the rhythm of daily life, all of it has become yours.
But then, out of nowhere, the old country tugs at your heart. A song drifting from an open bar, the smell of bread baking, a handwritten letter from someone back home—suddenly, memories you thought had faded come rushing back.
You find yourself caught in the middle, not fully at home in either place. At work, you get respect, maybe even friendship, but there’s always this faint sense of being slightly apart. The inside jokes you don’t quite understand, the holidays that don’t mean much to you, the family stories that started long before you ever arrived.
And at home, those phone calls with family—they’re bittersweet. You hear about a cousin’s wedding, a neighbor passing away, a sibling’s new job. Life keeps moving without you, and you’re left feeling both grateful to have your own life and a bit sad to be missing theirs.
One winter, he finally saves enough to visit Ireland. That trip back is full of both excitement and anxiety. When he steps off the train in his old village, there are hugs and laughter, but also a sense of distance. The streets feel smaller now. The faces are older. He realizes he’s changed—and so has home.
Conversations don’t flow as easily. The years apart make it hard to find the right words, or to slip into old routines. A neighbor who used to be a childhood friend asks, “Are you happy in America?” And that question just hangs in the air.
He tries to explain the mix of pride and loneliness, the opportunities and the things he’s lost along the way. Most people don’t realize how tough it is to belong to two places at once. And during the visit, he comes to see that home isn’t just a spot on a map—it’s a feeling. And sometimes, it’s a feeling that’s hard to get back.
When he returns to America, there’s a new understanding. That longing for home—it’ll always be there in some way, but it doesn’t have to take over his life. He starts to weave the old and the new together, making peace with the in-between.
The city’s skyline at dusk, the laughter of close friends, the comfort of familiar foods—these become his anchors.
And maybe that’s the heart of it: belonging isn’t really about fitting in perfectly. It’s about learning to find comfort in those in-between spaces, and making peace with all the pieces of yourself.
